text: A “3D calculator” could mean a few different tools, so I want to pin down the core job first. Which of these is closest to what you want?

suggestions: Volume and surface area of 3D shapes
A normal calculator with a 3D-styled keypad
Vector and coordinate math in 3D space
Something else — I'll describe it

text: Vector and coordinate math in 3D space
Vector and coordinate math it is. Which operations should be the must-haves on day one?

suggestions: Dot and cross product, magnitude, normalize, and angle between two vectors
Add, subtract, scale, plus distance, midpoint, and Cartesian/spherical conversion
Those vector ops plus a live 3D arrow view of the inputs and result
Rotation, scale, and translation of a point, with the matrix shown

text: Dot and cross product, magnitude, normalize, and angle between two vectors
Those five operations are the core. What should the app remember between visits?

suggestions: A short history of recent calculations you can reopen
Named vectors you save and reuse (like “up” or “velocity”)
Both a calculation history and a small library of named vectors
Nothing saved — just the two vectors you type in right now

text: all of above, and with threejs visualisations
History and a named-vector library, plus a live 3D view of the arrows. What should that screen feel like?

suggestions: Dark workspace: bright arrows on a black grid, numbers in a side panel
Light graph-paper page with a small 3D inset beside the inputs
Split layout: calculations on the left, a large 3D view on the right
Mostly the 3D scene, with compact floating readouts for the results

text: Split layout: calculations on the left, a large 3D view on the right
One last check before I lock the approach. What should count as “done” for this first version?

suggestions: Angles in degrees, results to about 3 decimal places, desktop-first
Radians and fuller precision, aimed at students checking homework
Works fully offline in one browser tab, no account
Show one operation’s result at a time so the panel stays easy to scan

text: You’ll get one polished workspace for 3D vector math: enter or pick two vectors on the left, run dot product, cross product, magnitude, normalize, or the angle between them, and watch the arrows update in a large view on the right. A named-vector library and a short history stay in the browser so you can reopen them later. The 3D view is a small vanilla canvas scene (grid, axis triad, color-coded arrows) so it stays on the fixed no-dependency stack. Angles show in degrees, rounded to three decimal places.

meta.title: 3D Vector Calculator
meta.pitch: Compute dot product, cross product, magnitude, normalize, and the angle between two 3D vectors, with a live arrow view.
features: Dot product, cross product, magnitude, normalize, and angle between two vectors
Split workspace: inputs and results on the left, large 3D arrow view on the right
Named vector library you can save and reuse
Recent calculation history you can reopen
approach: One page: left column for vector entry, the operation, the numeric result, the library, and history; right column for the 3D view
Vanilla canvas perspective view with a grid, an axis triad, and color-coded arrows for both inputs and the result, with no Three.js because the app cannot add npm packages
Angles in degrees, shown to three decimal places; a zero-length vector shows a clear message instead of a bogus angle
Named vectors and history persist in localStorage
screens: Workspace: calculation panel, library, and history on the left; large 3D view on the right
meta.look: Polished split layout: a calm dark calculation panel beside a large dark viewport with a light grid and brightly colored vector arrows
openRisks: Three.js was requested, but this stack has zero npm dependencies, so the 3D view is a custom canvas renderer rather than Three.js
Degrees and three decimal places are defaults; radians or more precision would change the result panel

text: Judge round 1: 4.3/5 — Approve. Recorded assessment replay. Approve after a small revision. Sequencing, fixtures, and the zero-dependency split are solid enough to build; specify when history rows are written and how the vector cap overflows, and pin light-grid camera defaults so the viewport matches the confirmed look.
